Content: Based on the SWS Versions Data Table, the student claims that SWS Version `Y` would be most effective at reducing damage to the spacecraft’s rear wall when space debris collides with the SWS bumper wall.
Which statement supports the student’s claim?

A.Choice: The collision with thicker walls would break the debris into smaller pieces and increase the speed of the debris as it travels a greater distance from the bumper wall to the rear wall.

Key.Rationale: Smaller pieces of debris would have a smaller mass, causing a decrease in speed.

B.Choice: The collision with thicker walls would break the debris into smaller pieces and reduce the speed of the debris as it travels a greater distance from the bumper wall to the rear wall.

Key.Rationale: Breaking up the debris into smaller pieces (smaller mass) and reducing the speed of the debris would reduce the net force of the collision.

C.Choice: The collision with thicker walls would break the rear wall into pieces, while the debris stays intact, and reduce the speed of the debris as it travels a greater distance from the bumper wall to the rear wall.

Key.Rationale: The collision with thicker walls would break any remaining debris into pieces instead of breaking the rear wall, and any intact debris would increase in speed.

D.Choice: The collision with thicker walls would break the rear wall into pieces, while the debris stays intact, and increase the speed of the debris as it travels a greater distance from the bumper wall to the rear wall.

Key.Rationale: The speed of the debris would decrease, not increase, because the collision with thicker walls would break any remaining debris into pieces instead of breaking the rear wall.

Content: Based on the information, which statement describes how an SWS should be designed so that it `bbtext(best)` shields the spacecraft from a collision with space debris?

A.Choice: Decrease the thickness of the rear wall so that the debris has less material to contact when it collides with the SWS.

Key.Rationale: Decreasing the thickness of the rear wall would limit how much the shield reduces the acceleration of any remaining solid debris, so this would not help shield the spacecraft from a collision with debris.

B.Choice: Increase the amount of material between the bumper wall and rear wall to reduce the force or forces in the collision.

Key.Rationale: Adding more Nextel and Kevlar layers between the bumper wall and rear wall would improve how much the shield reduces the acceleration of the debris, so that the force of the collision would be reduced and therefore rear wall damage would be reduced.

C.Choice: Decrease the number of Kevlar layers so that the bumper wall and the rear wall are closer together when the debris collides with the SWS.

Key.Rationale: Reducing the amount of material that the space debris would collide with would limit how much the shield reduces the acceleration of the debris, so this would not be an improvement to reduce rear wall damage.

D.Choice: Increase the mass of the bumper wall and rear wall to be similar to that of typical debris so that the force or forces in the collision are balanced.

Key.Rationale: Students may have the misconception that action-reaction forces can balance each other out, when this is not the case since these forces are between two different objects (the debris and the walls of the SWS).

Content: Which statement `text(best)` describes what scientists should consider when designing SWS devices?

A.Choice: If multiple versions of SWS devices are built, there can be many trials in which an object collides with a device.

Key.Rationale: SWS device design is an iterative process, where scientists consider alternate design pathways to improve the effectiveness of the SWS device.

B.Choice: After SWS devices collide with an object, the devices must be destroyed before any more devices can be built.

Key.Rationale: Scientists develop SWS devices through the design process so they can revisit how earlier devices were built and refine the design of the device instead of starting from scratch with a new design.

C.Choice: The `text(first)` of several SWS devices built is the most effective at protecting objects from being damaged during a collision between an object and the device.

Key.Rationale: Scientists designing an SWS device work to improve upon their initial designs, rather than assuming that the `text(first)` solution is the best solution.

D.Choice: Building SWS devices with the most expensive materials will make those devices most effective at reducing damage from a collision with an object.

Key.Rationale: The cost of an SWS device is a design constraint, as space missions typically operate within strict budget limits.

Content: The teams decided to investigate the effects of mass on the force needed to pull the shopping cart.
What could the students change in the investigation to make the cart go faster?

A.Choice: Put more mass in the cart.

Key.Rationale: Putting more mass in the cart will make the cart heavier and thereby harder to pull making it slower.

B.Choice: Put less mass in the cart.

Key.Rationale: Putting less mass in the cart will make the cart lighter and therefore go faster.

C.Choice: Use a longer rope to pull the shopping cart.

Key.Rationale: Using a different rope will not make the cart lighter and thereby easier to pull.

D.Choice: Use a larger shopping cart.

Key.Rationale: The shopping carts will have the same relative mass thereby this would not change the outcome of the investigation.

Content: The students noticed the surface they were racing on had different sized rocks on it. They wondered if the rocks being in the way would affect their race.
Which explanation `bbtext(best)` describes how the rocks will affect the shopping cart?

A.Choice: Only the big rocks will affect the shopping cart because the force of the rocks will be going in the same direction as the shopping cart’s wheels when it hits them.

Key.Rationale: The big rocks will affect the shopping cart but so will the small rocks because the rocks have an opposite net force as the shopping cart’s wheels upon impact.

B.Choice: Only the small rocks will affect the shopping cart because the force of the rocks will be going in the same direction as the shopping cart’s wheels when it hits them.

Key.Rationale: The small rocks will affect the shopping cart but so will the big rocks because the rocks have an opposite net force to the shopping cart’s wheels upon impact.

C.Choice: None of the rocks will affect the shopping cart because the rocks have `text(zero)` force.

Key.Rationale: The shopping cart could roll over some of the rocks but all the rocks will slow down the shopping cart because the rocks have an opposite net force to the shopping cart’s wheels upon impact.

D.Choice: All the rocks will affect the shopping cart because the force of the rocks will be going in the opposite direction as the shopping cart’s wheels when it hits them.

Key.Rationale: All the rocks will affect the shopping cart because the rocks have an opposite net force to the shopping cart’s wheels upon impact.

Content: Based on the data in the chart which `text(two)` runners should the Green Team select to win the race and why?

A.Choice: Runners `2` and `3`, because together they have the lowest pull force and slowest time.

Key.Rationale: Runners `2` and `3` have a combined pull force of `17.5` `text(N)` and an average time of `6.45` `text(s)`.

B.Choice: Runners `1` and `3`, because together they have the highest pull force and fastest time.

Key.Rationale: Runners `1` and `3` have a combined pull force of `22.2` `text(N)` and an average time of `4.9` `text(s)`, making them the fastest and the strongest pull force.

C.Choice: Runners `4` and `1`, because together they have the lowest pull force and fastest time.

Key.Rationale: Runners `4` and `1` have a combined pull force of `13.1` `text(N)` and an average time of `6.3` `text(s)`.

D.Choice: Runners `2` and `4`, because together they have the highest pull force and slowest time.

Key.Rationale: Runners `2` and `4` have a combined pull force of `8.4` `text(N)` and an average time of `7.85` `text(s)`.

Content: The student studies the Measuring Wave Characteristics diagram to find the amplitude of the wave in the tank. The student wants to draw a line showing where the amplitude of the wave is.
Based on the diagram, where should the amplitude of the wave be drawn?

A.Choice: The amplitude line should be drawn `text(halfway)` between the `0` and `25` `text(cm)` lines on the `ytext(-axis)`.

Key.Rationale: This represents the height of the crest but the amplitude is found by looking at the difference in the trough height and the crest height and dividing it in `text(half)`.

B.Choice: The amplitude line should be drawn at the `20` `text(cm)` line on the `ytext(-axis)`.

Key.Rationale: This height represents the trough, but the amplitude is found by looking at the differences in the trough height and the crest height and dividing it in `text(half)`.

C.Choice: The amplitude line should be drawn `text(halfway)` between the `20` and `25` `text(cm)` lines on the `ytext(-axis)`.

Key.Rationale: From trough to crest the wave is `5.0` `text(cm)`. The amplitude would be `text(half)` of the total height, which is `2.5` `text(cm)`.

D.Choice: The amplitude line should be drawn at the `25` `text(cm)` line on the `ytext(-axis)`.

Key.Rationale: This represents the height of the crest but the amplitude is found by looking at the difference in the trough height and the crest height and dividing it in `text(half)`.

Content: The student thinks about the waves on the lake being `text(two)` times higher than the day before.
How could the student cause the waves in the wave tank to become `text(two)` times higher?

A.Choice: Change the energy input from the motor to `text(one-quarter)` the original amount.

Key.Rationale: This is the taking the energy of the wave and making it reversely proportional to the square of the amplitude.

B.Choice: Change the energy input from the motor to `text(one-half)` the original amount.

Key.Rationale: This is taking the energy of the wave and making it reversely proportional to the amplitude.

C.Choice: Change the energy input from the motor to `text(two)` times the original amount.

Key.Rationale: This is taking the energy of the wave and making it proportional to the amplitude.

D.Choice: Change the energy input from the motor to `text(four)` times the original amount.

Key.Rationale: The energy of the wave is proportional to the square of the amplitude. If the height of a water wave is `text(doubled)`, `text(each wave)` will have `text(four)` times the energy.

Content: This question has `bbtext(two)` parts. Be sure to answer both parts of the question.

The student wants to make `text(two)` wave models. `text(One)` wave model will represent a decrease in wavelength without changing the amplitude. The other wave model will represent an increase in frequency with a change in the amplitude.

B.Choice: problems/OKG8S/media/9g.jpg

Content: Which statement is supported by the data in the `text(two)` graphs?

A.Choice: Forams of all sizes had more food sources in the Cretaceous period.

Key.Rationale: The student may think that the greater variety of Cretaceous forams indicates that were more food sources.

B.Choice: Forams with a larger size had more predators in the Cretaceous period.

Key.Rationale: The student may think that the greater variety of Cretaceous forams indicates that were more predators.

C.Choice: Forams with a smaller size had a survival advantage in the Tertiary period.

Key.Rationale: The average foram size decreased in the Tertiary period, which indicates that smaller size was an advantage.

D.Choice: Forams that were mid-sized had a higher reproductive rate in the Tertiary period.

Key.Rationale: The student may read the Cretaceous graph and may think the data reflects reproductive rates.

Content: Based on the information, how are the foram fossils from the `text(two)` time periods different?

A.Choice: The Cretaceous fossils are found in more locations than the Tertiary fossils.

Key.Rationale: The student may think that the different rocks come from different locations.

B.Choice: The Cretaceous fossils show a greater variety of body size than the Tertiary fossils.

Key.Rationale: The Tertiary graph shows sizes only from `0.01-0.19` `text(mm)`, while the Cretaceous graphs shows sizes from `0.01-0.59` `text(mm)`.

C.Choice: The Cretaceous fossils were more successful than Tertiary fossils at surviving the K-T extinction.

Key.Rationale: The student may be confused regarding the timing of the K-T extinction.

D.Choice: The Cretaceous fossils became more common and the Tertiary fossils disappeared from the fossil record.

Key.Rationale: The student may think that the `text(zero)` values in the graph indicate that the fossils disappeared.

Content: The students also gathered data about the number of fossilized foram species in rock layers at different heights above sea level from the Cretaceous and Tertiary time periods.
problems/OKG8S/media/12a.jpg
What is the `bbtext(most likely)` reason for the difference in the number of foram species in the layers from `3` to `5` `text(meters)` above sea level?

A.Choice: Individual forams became different species until the time of the K-T extinction.

Key.Rationale: The student may think that individuals become different species.

B.Choice: The number of foram species decreased steadily until the time of the K-T extinction.

Key.Rationale: The student may think that moving down from the surface is going forward in time rather than in reverse.

C.Choice: The surviving foram species diversified to fill the available habitats after the K-T extinction.

Key.Rationale: The number of species increases from layers `3-5` indicating that diversification occurred.

D.Choice: Several foram species moved from other habitats in the world to this location after the K-T extinction.

Key.Rationale: The student may think that migration is the most likely explanation.

Content: Which conclusion could the student make that is supported by the data?

A.Choice: From `text(1974)-text(2010)`, thyme plants with the phenolic trait were more likely to be eaten than before `text(1974)`.

Key.Rationale: This is not supported by the data because average annual winter temperature increased by `text(2010)` and corresponded to an increase in the distribution of the phenolic trait in the thyme population, which suggests that individuals with this trait were surviving to reproduce.

B.Choice: From `text(1974)-text(2010)`, thyme plants changed their nonphenolic trait to a phenolic trait over their lifetimes.

Key.Rationale: Students may have the misconception that individuals can change their traits over their lifetimes, rather than the distribution of traits changing in a population over time due to natural selection.

C.Choice: From `text(1974)-text(2010)`, thyme plants with the phenolic trait were less likely to freeze to death than before `text(1974)`.

Key.Rationale: The percentage of thyme plants with the phenolic trait increased relative to the nonphenolic trait during the same time period when average annual winter temperatures increased, suggesting that the freezing risk was lowered enough for the phenolic trait to be beneficial for reducing predation risk in the thyme plant population.

D.Choice: From `text(1974)-text(2010)`, thyme plants with the phenolic trait were stronger than thyme plants with the nonphenolic trait.

Key.Rationale: Students may have the misconception that natural selection is driven by individuals being strong enough to survive (“survival of the fittest”) and that this explains why both phenolic and nonphenolic thyme plants are present in the `text(2010)` thyme population.

Content: Based on the data, which statement explains the distribution of the nonphenolic trait in the thyme population from `text(1974)-text(2010)`?

A.Choice: Thyme plants with the nonphenolic trait rapidly changed to gain the phenolic trait because the environment became colder over time.

Key.Rationale: Students may have the misconception that organisms can change their features to suit their environment.

B.Choice: Thyme plants with the nonphenolic trait did not use their ability to withstand freezing temperatures because the environment became warmer over time.

Key.Rationale: Students may have the misconception that traits that are not used become less frequent in a population over time.

C.Choice: The nonphenolic trait was more likely to be inherited by thyme plants over many generations because the nonphenolic trait is advantageous in a colder environment.

Key.Rationale: Students may not recognize that the phenolic trait is disadvantageous in a colder environment.

D.Choice: The nonphenolic trait was less likely to be inherited by thyme plants over many generations because the nonphenolic trait is not advantageous in a warmer environment.

Key.Rationale: Since the nonphenolic trait helps thyme plants survive freezing temperatures, the increase in average winter temperatures from `text(1974)-text(2010)` likely explains why the frequency of nonphenolic thyme plants decreased, since nonphenolic thyme plants are at greater risk of being eaten by predators than phenolic thyme plants.

Content: Based on the data, which table represents how the proportion of thyme plants with each trait would `bbtext(most likely)` change if the average `text(annual)` winter temperature steadily increased from `text(2010)` to `text(2050)`?

A.Choice: problems/OKG8S/media/15a.jpg

Key.Rationale: If average `text(annual)` winter temperature continued to increase, it’s likely that phenolic thyme plants that can deter predators would be more likely to survive and reproduce than nonphenolic thyme plants, so the frequency of phenolic thyme plants in the population would likely increase while nonphenolic thyme plants would decrease.

B.Choice: problems/OKG8S/media/15b.jpg

Key.Rationale: If average `text(annual)` winter temperatures continued to increase, it’s likely that phenolic thyme plants that can deter predators would be more likely to survive and reproduce than nonphenolic thyme plants, so the frequency of nonphenolic thyme plants in the population would likely decrease, not increase.

C.Choice: problems/OKG8S/media/15c.jpg

Key.Rationale: If average `text(annual)` winter temperatures continued to increase, it’s likely that phenolic thyme plants that can deter predators would be more likely to survive and reproduce than nonphenolic thyme plants, so the frequency of phenolic thyme plants in the population would likely increase, not decrease.

D.Choice: problems/OKG8S/media/15d.jpg

Key.Rationale: Based on the frequency of thyme plants with the phenolic trait increasing and the nonphenolic trait decreasing with an increase in average `text(annual)` winter temperature, a further increase in average winter temperatures would be likely to further provide phenolic thyme plants with a survival advantage against predation.

Content: Based on the Position of `text(Earth)` in Orbit Around `text(Sun)` in `text(December)` model, which model best represents the position of `text(Earth)` relative to the `text(Sun)` in `text(June)`?

A.Choice: problems/OKG8S/media/16a.jpg

Key.Rationale: This model correctly represents the position of `text(Earth)` and the `text(Sun)` in `text(June)` because at this time `text(Earth’s)` North Pole is tilted toward the `text(Sun)` and `text(Earth’s)` South Pole is tilted away from the `text(Sun)`.

B.Choice: problems/OKG8S/media/16b.jpg

Key.Rationale: This model does not represent the position of `text(Earth)` and the `text(Sun)` in `text(June)` because it does not provide evidence that `text(each hemisphere)` receives different intensities of sunlight.

C.Choice: problems/OKG8S/media/16c.jpg

Key.Rationale: This model does not represent the position of `text(Earth)` and the `text(Sun)` in `text(June)` because the model shows the `text(Sun)` shining on both hemispheres rather than showing a difference in the intensity of sunlight `text(each hemisphere)` receives.

D.Choice: problems/OKG8S/media/16d.jpg

Key.Rationale: This model represents the position of `text(Earth)` and the `text(Sun)` at a time that better reflects the winter months on `text(Earth)` since `text(Earth’s)` South Pole is tilted toward the Sun and `text(Earth’s)` North Pole is tilted away from the `text(Sun)`.

Content: Based on the Position of `text(Earth)` in Orbit Around `text(Sun)` in `text(December)` model, which statement explains why winter occurs at different times of the year between hemispheres?

A.Choice: `text(Earth)` is relatively farther away from the `text(Sun)` when winter occurs on `text(Earth)`.

Key.Rationale: Students may have the misconception that the seasons are caused by `text(Earth’s)` general proximity to the `text(Sun)` (when `text(Earth)` is far away from the `text(Sun)` it is winter because it is colder).

B.Choice: `text(Earth)` orbits the `text(Sun)` slowly so that throughout the year global temperatures are colder when winter occurs.

Key.Rationale: Students may have the misconception that the rate at which `text(Earth)` orbits the `text(Sun)` primarily affects the seasons throughout the year.

C.Choice: `text(Earth)` has a tilted axis that affects when winter occurs on `text(Earth)` due to `text(Earth’s)` relative position while orbiting the `text(Sun)` throughout the year.

Key.Rationale: Since `text(Earth)` has a tilted axis as it orbits the `text(Sun)`, there is a differential intensity of sunlight on different parts of `text(Earth)` throughout the year.

D.Choice: `text(Earth)` spins relative to the `text(Sun)`, which affects when winter occurs due to `text(Earth)` facing the `text(Sun)` in the same direction as it spins throughout the year.

Key.Rationale: Students may have the misconception that `text(Earth’s)` spin primarily affects the seasons throughout the year.

Content: Which statement describes how the student could improve the Position of `text(Earth)` in Orbit Around `text(Sun)` in `text(December)` model to explain the seasons on `text(Earth)` in `text(December)`?

A.Choice: Show that the Southern and Northern Hemispheres receive high-intensity sunlight from the `text(Sun)`.

Key.Rationale: This would indicate that both hemispheres are experiencing summer in `text(December)`, but based on the table, the Northern Hemisphere is experiencing winter and the Southern Hemisphere is experiencing summer.

B.Choice: Show that the Southern and Northern Hemispheres receive low-intensity sunlight from the `text(Sun)`.

Key.Rationale: This would indicate that both hemispheres are experiencing winter in `text(December)`, but based on the table, the Northern Hemisphere is experiencing winter and the Southern Hemisphere is experiencing summer.

C.Choice: Show that the `text(Sun)` shines lower-intensity light on the Southern Hemisphere than on the Northern Hemisphere.

Key.Rationale: Based on the table, this would better represent `text(Earth)` in the month of `text(June)` since it would reflect summer in the Northern Hemisphere and winter in the Southern Hemisphere.

D.Choice: Show that the `text(Sun)` shines higher-intensity light on the Southern Hemisphere than on the Northern Hemisphere.

Key.Rationale: The table indicates that in `text(December)` it is winter in the Northern Hemisphere and summer in the Southern Hemisphere, so the model should show that this is due to each hemisphere receiving different intensities of sunlight at this time of the year.

Content: The students want to make a model to compare the size of the `text(three)` objects in the table.
According to the data, which model `bbtext(best)` shows the difference in sizes of the objects?

A.Choice: problems/OKG8S/media/19a.jpg

B.Choice: problems/OKG8S/media/19b.jpg

C.Choice: problems/OKG8S/media/19c.jpg

Key.Rationale: Although the watermelon is bigger than the orange, it is not enough larger to accurately reflect the difference in sizes between the `text(Sun)` and `text(Saturn)`. Also, the apple is almost the same size as the orange so a much smaller fruit should have been chosen.

Content: After viewing the models, the student claims that `text(Titan)` only orbits `text(Saturn)` and `text(Saturn)` only orbits the `text(Sun)`.
Which statement `bbtext(best)` evaluates the student’s claim?

A.Choice: The student is correct because only `text(Saturn)` is shown orbiting the `text(Sun)` in the model.

Key.Rationale: The student making the claim has not taken into account the limitations of the model or that the model is only showing `text(one)` interaction.

B.Choice: The student is correct because all moons orbit planets and `text(Titan)` is classified as a moon.

Key.Rationale: Although moons do orbit planets, they also orbit the `text(Sun)` as the planet orbits the `text(Sun)`.

C.Choice: The student is incorrect because all objects in the solar system orbit the `text(Sun)` because it has the largest mass.

Key.Rationale: All objects in the solar system orbit the `text(Sun)`, even if they orbit another object because the `text(Sun’s)` mass is so large that all objects within the solar system orbit its mass.

D.Choice: The student is incorrect because `text(Saturn)` has less mass than the `text(Sun)`, which causes `text(Titan)` to only orbit the `text(Sun)`.

Key.Rationale: `text(Saturn)` does have less mass than the `text(Sun)`, but `text(Saturn)` is closer to the `text(Sun)`, which is why it orbits `text(Saturn)` as well as the `text(Sun)`.

Content: This question has `bbtext(two)` parts. Be sure to answer both parts of the question.
Which sentence `bbtext(best)` compares the gravitational force between the pairs of objects?

A.Choice: The gravitational force between `text(Titan)` and `text(Saturn)` is greater than the gravitational force between `text(Titan)` and the `text(Sun)` because of the masses of the interacting objects.

Key.Rationale: The table shows that the combined masses of `text(Titan)` and `text(Saturn)` are smaller than the combined masses of `text(Titan)` and the `text(Sun)`.

B.Choice: The gravitational force between `text(Titan)` and `text(Saturn)` is greater than the gravitational force between `text(Titan)` and the `text(Sun)` because of the distances between the interacting objects.

Key.Rationale: The orbital model shows that `text(Titan)` orbits `text(Saturn)`, which shows that the gravitational force between them is stronger. The decreased distance is why the gravitational force is stronger even though the table shows that the mass of the `text(Sun)` is much larger than the mass of `text(Saturn)`.

C.Choice: The gravitational force between `text(Titan)` and `text(Saturn)` is less than the gravitational force between `text(Titan)` and the `text(Sun)` because of the masses of the interacting objects.

Key.Rationale: The orbital model shows that `text(Titan)` orbits `text(Saturn)`, meaning that the gravitational attraction is greater than the gravitational attraction of the `text(Sun)` and `text(Titan)`. The table shows that the combined masses of `text(Titan)` and `text(Saturn)` are smaller than the combined masses of `text(Titan)` and the `text(Sun)`.

D.Choice: The gravitational force between `text(Titan)` and `text(Saturn)` is less than the gravitational force between `text(Titan)` and the `text(Sun)` because of the distances between the interacting objects.

Key.Rationale: The orbital model shows that `text(Titan)` orbits `text(Saturn)`, meaning that the gravitational attraction is greater than the gravitational attraction of the `text(Sun)` and `text(Titan)`.

Content: Which sentence `bbtext(best)` compares the gravitational force between the pairs of objects?

A.Choice: The gravitational force between the `text(Sun)` and `text(Saturn)` is greater than the gravitational force between the `text(Sun)` and `text(Titan)` because of the masses of the interacting objects.

Key.Rationale: The data table shows that the average distance between `text(Titan)` and `text(Saturn)` to the `text(Sun)` is the same. Because `text(Saturn)` has more mass, there will be more gravitational attraction between `text(Saturn)` and the `text(Sun)` than `text(Titan)` and the `text(Sun)`.

B.Choice: The gravitational force between the `text(Sun)` and `text(Saturn)` is greater than the gravitational force between the `text(Sun)` and `text(Titan)` because of the distances between the interacting objects.

Key.Rationale: Distance between the interacting objects is not different according to the data table, so the reasoning behind the greater gravitational force is incorrect.

C.Choice: The gravitational force between the `text(Sun)` and `text(Saturn)` is less than the gravitational force between the `text(Sun)` and `text(Titan)` because of the masses of the interacting objects.

Key.Rationale: Since `text(Saturn)` and `text(Titan)` are the same distance from the `text(Sun)`, the masses of the interacting objects will have the effect on the difference in the gravitational forces. Gravitational force increases with mass, so `text(Saturn)` and the `text(Sun)` will have a greater gravitational force between them.

D.Choice: The gravitational force between the `text(Sun)` and `text(Saturn)` is less than the gravitational forces between the `text(Sun)` and `text(Titan)` because of the distances between the interacting objects.

Key.Rationale: Distance between the interacting objects is not different according to the data table, so the reasoning behind the greater gravitational force is incorrect.
